H1_primary: disclosure precision: the fast-class rate interval is narrower than 0.25 AND both price-only rate intervals are wider than 0.25; success if this holds in at least 75% of included markets
H2: trend following: the fast-class response to returns w is positive with interval above 0, in at least 75% of markets
H3: classes differ: the fast class has a shorter memory than the slow class (interval of r_fast - r_slow below 0), in at least half of the markets

classes.DIS: fast = managed money, slow = producer/merchant, dealer = swap dealers
classes.TFF: fast = leveraged funds, slow = asset managers, dealer = dealers

data: CFTC public reporting API (futures-only reports), all weekly reports through 2026-10-13; prices: Binance spot daily close (BTC, ETH); Yahoo Finance daily close for the others: S&P 500 index, 10-year yield (enters as minus the change), EUR/USD, USD/JPY (inverted), and front-month crude-oil and natural-gas futures. Class position n = (long - short) / open interest; weekly return from the last price on or before the report date (at most 4 days old); only consecutive weekly reports.
inclusion: a market enters if it has at least 150 usable weeks
inference: moving-block bootstrap, 13-week blocks, 2,000 draws; 95% percentile intervals
price_only_model: weekly returns on 12 own lags (OLS), then a two-exponential kernel fitted on a 0.02 grid of rates in [0, 0.99]
question: Does legally mandated class-tagged disclosure (CFTC Commitments of Traders) pin down trader-class memory rates that prices alone leave unrestricted, and do the classes behave as the cohort model predicts?
relation: Paper 1 Table tab:disc (Binance long/short ratios, Part 6) is the first disclosure regime; this is the second.
runs: C4 is run once; every run is counted in prereg/test_set_unlocks_p11.json
tagged_model: n_t = alpha + r * n_{t-1} + w * ret_t + e_t by OLS, for each class
